questions.question: Describe the mechanism of action and class of daptomycin.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action and class of daptomycin?

parts_raw.text: What is the MOA and class of daptomycin?

questions.model_answer: a) Class: cyclic lipopeptide. Mechanism: calcium-dependent binding of its lipophilic tail into the bacterial cell membrane causing rapid depolarization and potassium efflux, inhibiting intracellular DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis; bactericidal in a concentration-dependent manner. It is contraindicated for pneumonia because it is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant (though it may be used for pulmonary septic emboli from right-sided endocarditis).

cohort_answer.text: Lipopeptide: binds to the components of cell membrane rapid depolarization inhibiting intracellular synthesis of DNA/ RNA. Bactericidal in concentration dependent manner. Contraindicated in pneumonia, aside from embolic disease secondary to right-sided endocarditis

questions.question: Daptomycin.

parts.text: Why is it contraindicated in pulmonary infection?
Name the class to which it belongs.
Name two serious adverse reactions.

parts_raw.text: Why contraindicated in pulmonary infection?
Name class to which it belongs.
Name 2 serious adverse reactions.

questions.model_answer: a) Its antibacterial activity is abolished by binding to and inactivation by pulmonary surfactant, so it cannot treat pneumonia. b) Cyclic lipopeptide. c) (1) Skeletal muscle toxicity/rhabdomyolysis (dose-dependent CK elevation - discontinue if CK >1000 U/L with symptoms or >2000 U/L asymptomatic); (2) Eosinophilic pneumonia (typically after ~2 weeks of therapy).

cohort_answer.text: Pulmonary contraindication: antimicrobial activity abolished by interaction with pulmonary surfactant; also poor penetration to CNS, bone. Class: Lipopeptides (peak-MIC ratio, 24-hr AUC/MIC, post-antibiotic effect; dose 4-6mg/kg SSTI, 8-10mg/kg severe infections). Adverse reactions: Skeletal muscle toxicity (dose dependent, reversible - D/C if CK>1000 with symptoms or CK>2000 asymptomatic); Eosinophilic pneumonia (usually after 10 days therapy); also severe autoimmune thrombocytopenia/neutropenia, CDI, peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, falsely elevated PT

parts_raw.text: What antimicrobial class does daptomycin belong to?

questions.model_answer: a) Cyclic lipopeptide. b) Calcium-dependent insertion of its lipophilic tail into the bacterial cell membrane; aggregation forms pores causing rapid depolarization and potassium efflux, arresting DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis and producing concentration-dependent bactericidal killing. c) (1) Respiratory/lung (pneumonia) - inactivated by pulmonary surfactant; (2) Central nervous system - poor penetration across the blood-brain barrier, especially with non-inflamed meninges.

cohort_answer.text: Class: lipopeptide. MOA: binds to cell membrane components, causes rapid depolarization; aggregation of daptomycin creates holes that leak ions out of the cell, causing cell death. Not used for: respiratory infections/pneumonia (inhibited by surfactant); CNS infections (does not cross blood-brain barrier, especially with non-inflamed meninges); also prostate.

cohort_answer.text: Class: Cyclic lipopeptide. Not to use for: Pneumonia - inactivated by pulmonary surfactant; MRSA infection in children <12 months old. If underlying myopathy/higher rates of rhabdo associated with baseline renal impairment, concomitant statin administration, and obesity. questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Daptomycin – cidal (high-dose 10–12 mg/kg preferred); (2) Linezolid – static; (3) Quinupristin-dalfopristin – cidal against E. faecium; (4) Tigecycline – static.

questions.question: A patient presents with MRSA bacteremia.

parts.text: Name 2 agents that are approved for MRSA bacteremia.
An echocardiogram shows a vegetation on a prosthetic valve. What agent would you add?

parts_raw.text: 2 agents that are approved for MRSA bacteremia.
An echo was performed, and the patient has a vegetation on a prosthetic valve. What agent to add?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg IV q12h). (2) Daptomycin (8-10 mg/kg IV q24h). b) Add rifampin (900 mg IV q24h or 300 mg PO q8h) for the duration of therapy, together with gentamicin (3 mg/kg IV q24h) for the first 2 weeks. Rifampin is added specifically because it helps kill bacteria adherent to the foreign/prosthetic material and must never be used alone (selects resistance at ~10^-6).

cohort_answer.text: Vancomycin; Daptomycin. || Rifampin (x6 weeks) + gent (x2 weeks).

questions.question_raw: Name the most likely mechanism of resistance

parts.text: Serratia marcescens resistant to ertapenem, imipenem AND meropenem, but susceptible to ceftriaxone.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa resistant to meropenem, but susceptible to imipenem.
Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin.
Enterococcus gallinarum resistant to vancomycin, but susceptible to teicoplanin.
Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime.

Staphylococcus aureus resistant to daptomycin

questions.model_answer: a) Class A carbapenemase (enzymatic inactivation), e.g., chromosomal SME (or OXA-48-type), which hydrolyzes carbapenems while sparing extended-spectrum cephalosporins. b) Upregulated efflux (MexAB-OprM) - meropenem is a substrate but imipenem is not; imipenem resistance would instead require OprD porin loss. c) Cell-membrane target alteration (increased net positive surface charge, e.g., mprF), reducing binding of calcium-dependent daptomycin. d) VanC ligase producing D-Ala-D-Ser termini - intrinsic, low-level vancomycin resistance in E. gallinarum with retained teicoplanin susceptibility. e) Derepression/hyperexpression of chromosomal AmpC combined with porin (permeability) loss.
questions.beyond_mandell: Detailed resistance mechanisms are covered in Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance), not this organism chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

questions.question: Daptomycin and linezolid.

parts.text: Give two similarities in pharmacokinetics and spectrum.
Give two differences in the same things.

parts_raw.text: A) Give 2 similarities in pharmacokinetic and spectrum
B) Give 2 differences in the same things

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Spectrum: both cover Gram-positive organisms including MRSA and VRE; (2) Both are eliminated at least partly renally (daptomycin ~80%, linezolid ~30%, requiring daptomycin dose adjustment in renal impairment). b) (1) Route/bioavailability: linezolid is available orally and IV with excellent oral bioavailability, whereas daptomycin is IV only and weight-based; (2) Site penetration: linezolid penetrates lung and CNS well and can treat pneumonia and meningitis, whereas daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant (no pneumonia) and penetrates CNS poorly. (Also: daptomycin is bactericidal vs linezolid bacteriostatic; linezolid additionally covers some mycobacteria.)

cohort_answer.text: A) Only PK similarity: renal excretion (30% linezolid, ~80% daptomycin). Spectrum: gram positive coverage incl MRSA, VRE. B) Protein binding: Dapto 90% vs Linezolid 31%. CNS penetration: Dapto poor vs Linezolid adequate. Pneumonia: Dapto poor vs Linezolid adequate. Spectrum: Dapto GP only, no mycobacteria vs Linezolid broad GP coverage, mycobacteria covered. Practicality: Dapto IV only, wt based, renal dosing vs Linezolid PO/IV, fixed dose, no renal dosing, high bioavailability.

questions.question: A patient with MRSA pneumonia (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistant, macrolide resistant) is switched from vancomycin to daptomycin and begins to deteriorate. Antibacterial mechanism of resistance.
questions.question_raw: Q41 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Pt with MRSA pneumonia (Septra R, Macrolides R), switched from vancomycin to daptomycin. Begins to get worse.

parts.text: Reason for treatment failure.
Two other drugs that could be used, if sensitive.

parts_raw.text: a) Reason for treatment failure
b) 2 other drugs that could be used, if sensitive

questions.model_answer: a) Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and therefore cannot be used to treat pneumonia - it fails to reduce bacterial burden in the lung. b) (1) Linezolid (shown superior to vancomycin in MRSA nosocomial pneumonia); (2) Ceftaroline (or, if susceptible, vancomycin at higher trough).

cohort_answer.text: a) Daptomycin antimicrobial activity inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, resulting in failure to reduce bacterial burden in bronchoalveolar pneumonia. b) Linezolid (ZEPHyR study showed superior to vancomycin in MRSA HAP); Telavancin; Ceftaroline; Ceftobiprole; Doxycycline.
